name: Meigs syndrome
aliases: ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion

clinicalPearls: Defined by the triad of a benign solid ovarian tumour, ascites, and a pleural effusion, all of which resolve after the tumour is removed
The classic tumour is an ovarian fibroma, though thecomas, Brenner tumours, and granulosa cell tumours may produce the same picture
The pleural effusion is more often right-sided, and both effusions are transudative and benign
CA-125 may be raised, which together with ascites and an adnexal mass can closely mimic advanced ovarian malignancy
The term pseudo-Meigs syndrome is used when a similar picture accompanies other ovarian or pelvic tumours
Recognising the syndrome avoids the assumption of disseminated malignancy and the inappropriate management that would follow
Complete surgical removal of the tumour is curative, with resolution of the ascites and pleural effusion
reference.pathophysiology: A benign solid ovarian tumour, most commonly a fibroma, becomes associated with the accumulation of ascitic fluid and a pleural effusion. The fluid is thought to arise from transudation or leakage from the surface of the tumour or its lymphatics into the peritoneal cavity, from where it passes to the pleural space through diaphragmatic lymphatic channels and defects. Because the effusions are secondary to the presence of the tumour rather than to malignant spread, they resolve once it is excised.
additionalDifferentials: Ovarian malignancy with malignant ascites and pleural effusions
Pseudo-Meigs syndrome from other pelvic tumours
Cirrhosis or heart failure causing ascites and effusion
Other causes of an exudative or transudative pleural effusion
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal and pelvic ultrasound demonstrating a solid ovarian mass
Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to define the mass and effusions
Serum CA-125, interpreted cautiously given its poor specificity in this setting
Analysis of pleural and ascitic fluid to confirm a benign, non-malignant nature
Histological examination of the excised tumour for definitive diagnosis
redFlags: A clinical and radiological picture indistinguishable from disseminated ovarian malignancy
A markedly raised CA-125 heightening concern for cancer
A large pleural effusion causing breathlessness or respiratory compromise
Any histological or cytological feature suggesting true malignancy
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; because the tumour is benign, complete surgical removal cures the condition and leads to full resolution of the ascites and pleural effusion.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the syndrome as advanced ovarian malignancy and instituting inappropriate treatment
Placing undue reliance on a raised CA-125 to infer malignancy
Failing to obtain fluid cytology to confirm the benign nature of the effusions
Not recognising that resolution of effusions after surgery supports the diagnosis
management: Perform complete surgical excision of the benign ovarian tumour, which is curative and resolves the effusions
Confirm the benign diagnosis by histological examination of the excised tumour
Provide therapeutic drainage of symptomatic ascites or pleural effusion for relief while awaiting surgery
Interpret a raised CA-125 cautiously and use imaging to avoid mistaking the syndrome for disseminated ovarian malignancy
Analyse pleural and ascitic fluid to confirm its benign, transudative nature
Confirm resolution of the ascites and pleural effusion after tumour removal
